title: Components
summary: Functional vs Class components, component lifecycle, composability, and UI modularity.

explanation.overview: Components are independent, reusable UI building blocks in React. Modern React favors Functional Components with Hooks over legacy Class Components.

sections.heading: Functional Components vs Class Components
sections.content: Functional components are JavaScript functions returning JSX. Class components extend `React.Component` and use lifecycle methods (`componentDidMount`, `shouldComponentUpdate`).
bulletPoints: Functional: Cleaner syntax, Hook support, no `this` binding complexity.
Class: Legacy syntax, explicit lifecycle methods, state inside `this.state`.

sections.heading: Component Composition & Modularity
sections.content: React promotes component composition over inheritance. Smaller single-responsibility components are composed into complex application UI trees.
bulletPoints: Single Responsibility Principle: Keep components focused on one task.
Container vs Presentational pattern: Decouple stateful logic from UI markup.

keyTakeaways: Use Functional components with Hooks for modern React development.
Favor component composition over class inheritance.
Keep components small and single-purpose for easy maintenance.

codeExamples.title: Functional Component with Props
codeExamples.description: A clean functional React component using TypeScript props.

mcqs.question: What is the primary benefit of Functional Components with Hooks in modern React?
options: Cleaner stateful logic reuse without class syntax or `this` complexity
mcqs.explanation: Functional components eliminate `this` context binding bugs and enable custom hook logic reuse.

mcqs.question: What architectural pattern does React recommend for code reuse across UI elements?
mcqs.explanation: React strongly recommends composition using props and children rather than OOP inheritance.

mcqs.question: Which legacy class method handles initial side-effects after component DOM mounting?
mcqs.explanation: `componentDidMount` runs immediately after a class component inserts into the DOM.

mcqs.question: What must a React component function return?
options: JSX element tree, null, or valid React node
mcqs.explanation: React component render functions must return valid JSX elements, fragments, arrays, primitives, or `null`.

mcqs.question: How should Presentational components be designed compared to Container components?
options: Focus strictly on UI rendering based on props received
mcqs.explanation: Presentational components focus purely on rendering UI based on props without managing complex async state.

title: JSX
summary: JavaScript XML syntax extension, compilation to React.createElement, embedding expressions, and Fragments.

explanation.overview: JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript that looks like HTML. Transpilers like Babel convert JSX tags into `React.createElement()` calls at build time.

sections.heading: JSX Compilation Mechanics
sections.content:
JSX tag `
Hello
` compiles to `React.createElement('div', { className: 'box' }, 'Hello')`. JSX attributes use camelCase (`className`, `htmlFor`).
bulletPoints: Transpilation: Converted by Babel/SWC to `React.createElement` or `jsx()` runtime.
Attribute Naming: Use `className` for HTML class, `htmlFor` for label for.
Sanitization: React escapes strings embedded in JSX automatically to prevent XSS.

sections.heading: Embedding Expressions & React Fragments
sections.content: JavaScript expressions can be embedded inside curly braces `{}`. React Fragments `<>...</>` group multiple sibling elements without introducing extra DOM container nodes.
bulletPoints: Curly Braces: `{ 2 + 2 }`, `{ isLogged ? <Dash /> : <Login /> }`.
Fragments: `<React.Fragment>` or `<>` avoids clean wrapper DOM bloat.
Keys: Fragments require `<React.Fragment key={id}>` when mapping lists.

keyTakeaways: JSX compiles down to JavaScript function calls.
React automatically sanitizes string values in JSX against XSS.
Use Fragments to avoid unnecessary DOM wrapper divs.

codeExamples.title: JSX Expressions & Fragment
codeExamples.description: Conditional rendering, array map, and React Fragment.

mcqs.question:
What does JSX `

Hi

` compile into under the hood?
mcqs.explanation: Build transpilers transform JSX elements into `React.createElement()` calls.

mcqs.question: Why is `className` used in JSX instead of standard HTML `class`?
options: `class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript
Browsers do not support HTML class
mcqs.explanation: Because JSX is JavaScript, `class` is a reserved language keyword, requiring `className`.

mcqs.question: How does React handle embedded string variables in JSX against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
options: Automatically escapes embedded string expressions before rendering
mcqs.explanation: React escapes all values rendered inside JSX by default to prevent XSS injection attacks.

mcqs.question: What is primary advantage of React Fragments `<>...</>`?
options: Groups sibling elements without adding extra wrapper nodes to the DOM tree
mcqs.explanation: Fragments render multiple child elements without creating useless container `<div>` tags.

mcqs.question: Which shorthand syntax renders conditional UI in JSX when condition is true?
mcqs.explanation: Logical AND `{ condition && <Element /> }` renders `<Element />` if `condition` evaluates to true.

title: Props
summary: Passing data downward, immutable read-only props, children prop, and default prop values.

explanation.overview: Props (short for properties) are read-only inputs passed from parent to child components, establishing a unidirectional data flow.

sections.heading: Unidirectional Data Flow & Immutability
sections.content: Props flow strictly top-down. A child component must never mutate its received props directly.
bulletPoints: Read-only: Components behave like pure functions with respect to their props.
Prop Drilling: Passing props through multiple layout component layers.
Callback Props: Child triggers parent updates by invoking function props.

sections.heading: The children Prop & Defaults
sections.content: `children` is a special prop that receives elements placed between component opening and closing tags. ES6 destructuring handles default prop values.
bulletPoints: `children`: Enables wrapper/modal component composition.
Default Props: `function Card({ variant = 'primary' })`.

keyTakeaways: Props are strictly read-only and immutable.
Data flows top-down (unidirectional).
Use `children` prop for layout wrapper components.

codeExamples.title: Passing Props & Callback Function
codeExamples.description: Child component calling parent handler via function prop.

mcqs.question: Can a child component directly mutate `props.title = 'New Title'`?
options: No, props are read-only and immutable inside receiving component
mcqs.explanation: Props are strictly immutable; mutating props breaks React unidirectional data flow model.

mcqs.question: What is 'Prop Drilling' in React?
options: Passing props down through multiple intermediary components that do not need them
mcqs.explanation: Prop drilling occurs when props must pass through multiple middle component layers to reach deep children.

mcqs.question: What does the special `children` prop represent in React?
options: Content nested between component opening and closing tags `<Card>{content}</Card>`
mcqs.explanation: `props.children` contains elements or text rendered inside component opening and closing tags.

mcqs.question: How should a child component notify its parent component about a user action?
options: Invoke a callback function passed down as a prop
mcqs.explanation: Parents pass handler functions as props; children call those callbacks to trigger parent state changes.

mcqs.question: How are default prop values handled cleanly in modern React functional components?
options: Using ES6 parameter default values in function signature `({ size = 'md' })`
mcqs.explanation: Modern React uses standard ES6 destructured parameter defaults directly in component signature.

title: State
summary: Component memory, state vs props, asynchronous state updates, and immutable state updates.

explanation.overview: State is component private memory that changes over time. When component state updates, React schedules a component re-render.

sections.heading: State vs Props
sections.content: Props are external inputs passed into a component. State is internal memory owned and managed directly within the component.
bulletPoints: Props: External, read-only from child perspective.
State: Internal, mutable via state updater functions (`setState` / `useState`).
Re-rendering: Changing state triggers component re-render cycle.

sections.heading: Immutable Updates & Asynchronous Batching
sections.content: React state updates are batched for performance. State must always be updated immutably using updater functions.
bulletPoints: Functional Updates: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` for state derived from prior state.
Object/Array State: Never mutate state objects directly; return fresh shallow copies `{ ...prev, key: val }`.

keyTakeaways: Updating state triggers component re-render.
Never mutate state directly (`state.count = 5` is invalid).
Use functional state updater `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` when next state depends on current state.

codeExamples.title: Immutable Object State Update
codeExamples.description: Updating nested object state using shallow copy spread.

mcqs.question: What happens when a component state is updated using its setter function?
options: React schedules a re-render of the component and its children
mcqs.explanation: Updating state notifies React to schedule a component re-render to reflect new state in UI.

mcqs.question: What is wrong with directly writing `user.name = 'Bob'` in a React stateful component?
options: React is unaware of direct mutation and will not trigger a re-render
mcqs.explanation: Direct state mutation skips React state update pipeline, failing to trigger re-render.

mcqs.question: When updating state based on previous state value, what is best practice?
mcqs.explanation: Functional updates ensure accurate updates when state calls are batched or asynchronous.

mcqs.question: What is automatic state batching in React 18?
options: Grouping multiple state updates into a single re-render pass even inside async promises/timeouts
mcqs.explanation: React 18 batches state updates across event handlers, promises, and timeouts into single re-renders.

mcqs.question: How should an array state `items` be updated when adding a new item `newItem`?
mcqs.explanation: Array state must be updated immutably using spread `[...items, newItem]` to create a new array reference.

title: Rendering
summary: Render phase vs Commit phase, virtual DOM tree comparison, triggering re-renders, and pure rendering.

explanation.overview: Rendering is the process where React calls components to determine what UI should look like. Rendering consists of Render Phase (calculating changes) and Commit Phase (updating real DOM).

sections.heading: Render Phase vs Commit Phase
sections.content: In Render Phase, React invokes components to generate new Virtual DOM tree. In Commit Phase, React applies minimal calculated DOM mutations to browser DOM.
bulletPoints: Render Phase: Pure computation, side-effect free, can be paused in Concurrent React.
Commit Phase: Synchronous DOM updates (`componentDidMount`, `useLayoutEffect`).

sections.heading: What Triggers a Component Re-render?
sections.content: A component re-renders whenever its internal state updates or parent component re-renders.
bulletPoints: State Change: Calling state updater.
Parent Re-render: Parent re-rendering forces children to re-render by default (unless memoized).
Context Change: Context provider value update re-renders all consumer components.

keyTakeaways: Render phase computes Virtual DOM; Commit phase updates real DOM.
Child components re-render when parent re-renders by default.
Keep render function body pure and side-effect free.

codeExamples.title: Pure Render Function Example
codeExamples.description: Component render function remaining pure without side-effects.

mcqs.question: What happens during React Render Phase?
options: Real browser DOM is wiped out
React calls component functions to construct new Virtual DOM tree and diff against previous tree
mcqs.explanation: Render Phase calls component functions to generate new Virtual DOM and calculate diffs.

mcqs.question: What occurs during React Commit Phase?
options: React applies calculated DOM mutations to real browser DOM
mcqs.explanation: Commit Phase applies Virtual DOM diff mutations synchronously into actual DOM nodes.

mcqs.question: What happens to child components when a parent component re-renders?
options: Children re-render by default unless wrapped in memoization like React.memo
mcqs.explanation: Parent component re-renders recursively trigger child component re-renders by default.

mcqs.question: Why must component render function bodies remain 'pure'?
options: Side-effects in render body cause unexpected behavior because React may call render multiple times or discard draft renders
mcqs.explanation: Render bodies can run multiple times in Concurrent React; side-effects belong inside `useEffect`.

mcqs.question: Does a component re-render if props passed to it remain identical but its parent re-renders?
options: Yes, by default unless child uses React.memo
mcqs.explanation: Un-memoized functional components re-render whenever parent re-renders regardless of prop equivalence.

title: Reconciliation
summary: Diffing algorithm, Virtual DOM comparisons, O(n) heuristics, and list item `key` prop rules.

explanation.overview: Reconciliation is React diffing algorithm that compares current Virtual DOM tree with previous tree to compute minimal real DOM operations required.

sections.heading: Heuristic Diffing Algorithm O(n)
sections.content:
General tree comparison is $O(n^3)$. React uses two $O(n)$ heuristic rules:
1. Elements of different types produce completely different trees (destroys and unmounts old subtree).
2. Keys distinguish list items across re-renders.
bulletPoints: Root Component Swap: Replacing `<div>` with `<span>` unmounts entire child subtree.
Same Element Type: React updates changed attributes without destroying DOM node.

sections.heading: Importance of List Keys
sections.content: Keys give array elements persistent identities across renders. Avoid array index keys when list items can be re-ordered, inserted, or filtered.
bulletPoints: Unique & Stable Keys: Use database IDs or unique item hashes.
Index Key Pitfall: Causes state corruption and incorrect input focus when items shift positions.

keyTakeaways: Reconciliation uses an efficient $O(n)$ diffing algorithm.
Changing element types unmounts and remounts entire subtrees.
Use unique, stable IDs as list keys instead of array indexes.

codeExamples.title: List Keys in React
codeExamples.description: Using unique ID as stable key for mapped list elements.

mcqs.question: What complexity order is React diffing heuristic algorithm?
mcqs.explanation: React heuristic diffing algorithm runs in linear time $O(n)$.

mcqs.question: What happens during reconciliation if a component root changes from `<div>` to `<section>`?
options: React completely unmounts old div subtree and mounts new section tree
mcqs.explanation: Changing DOM element types causes React to tear down and recreate entire subtree.

mcqs.question: Why is using array index `key={index}` problematic for dynamic lists that can be reordered?
options: Causes state bugs and unnecessary re-renders because indexes shift when items are reordered or deleted
mcqs.explanation: Shifting indexes misaligns item state with wrong DOM elements when list order changes.

mcqs.question: What is the Virtual DOM in React?
options: Lightweight in-memory JavaScript object representation of UI elements
mcqs.explanation: Virtual DOM is an in-memory JS object tree representing UI structure.

mcqs.question: What requirement must a React list `key` prop satisfy?
options: Must be globally unique across whole app
Must be unique among sibling elements in that specific array
mcqs.explanation: Keys need to be unique only among immediate sibling elements in mapped array.

title: useState
summary: State hook syntax, state initializers, lazy state initialization, and updater functions.

explanation.overview: `useState` is the core React hook for adding local state variables to functional components.

sections.heading: useState Syntax & Destructuring
sections.content: `const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue)` returns tuple of current state value and state updater function.
bulletPoints: Initial Value: Sets state for initial component render.
Tuple Destructuring: Standard convention `[value, setValue]`.
Re-render: Calling `setValue` triggers component re-render.

sections.heading: Lazy State Initialization
sections.content: If initial state requires expensive calculations, pass a initializer function `useState(() => expensiveCalc())`. The function executes only on initial mount.
bulletPoints: Lazy Init: `useState(() => getStoredData())` runs once on mount.
Eager Init: `useState(getStoredData())` runs calculation on every single re-render!

keyTakeaways: `useState` returns tuple `[state, setState]`.
Use functional initializers `useState(() => ...)` for expensive initial state computations.
Use functional updates `setState(prev => ...)` when next state depends on previous state.

codeExamples.title: Lazy Initializer & Functional State Update
codeExamples.description: Reading localStorage lazily on mount and incrementing state safely.

mcqs.question: What does `useState(0)` return?
mcqs.explanation: `useState` returns 2-element array: `[state, setState]`.

mcqs.question: What is advantage of lazy state initialization `useState(() => computeHeavyData())`?
options: Runs initializer function strictly once on initial component mount
mcqs.explanation: Passing function to `useState` executes initialization computation only during initial component mount.

mcqs.question: What happens if you call `setState(5)` twice in same event handler `setState(5); setState(5);`?
options: React batches update and re-renders component once because value did not change
mcqs.explanation: React checks value equality (`Object.is`); if state value does not change, re-render is skipped.

mcqs.question: Why is `setCount(count + 1)` three times in one handler wrong if you want count to increase by 3?
options: All 3 calls reference same captured `count` variable value in closure, incrementing by 1 total
mcqs.explanation: Calls use captured closure `count`; use `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` to queue sequential functional updates.

mcqs.question: Can `useState` hooks be called conditionally inside an `if` statement?
options: No, hooks must always be called unconditionally at top level of functional component
mcqs.explanation: React Rules of Hooks mandate calling hooks at top level unconditionally to preserve hook call order.

title: useEffect
summary: Side-effects, dependency array rules, cleanup functions, and lifecycle equivalence.

explanation.overview: `useEffect` performs side-effects (data fetching, subscriptions, DOM mutations, timers) in functional components after rendering.

sections.heading: Dependency Array Variations
sections.content:
Behavior depends on second argument dependency array:
1. No array: Runs after every render.
2. Empty array `[]`: Runs once after initial mount (like `componentDidMount`).
3. Dependency list `[a, b]`: Runs on mount and when `a` or `b` values change.
bulletPoints: No Array: Runs after every single render.
Empty `[]`: Runs once on mount.
Dependencies `[dep]`: Runs when `dep` changes.

sections.heading: Effect Cleanup Function
sections.content: Returning a function from `useEffect` registers a cleanup callback. Runs before effect re-executes and when component unmounts.
bulletPoints: Cleanup: Prevents memory leaks (clear timers, unsubscribe events, abort fetch).
Unmount: Runs cleanup function when component unmounts from DOM.

keyTakeaways: `useEffect` handles side-effects after render commit phase.
Always declare all reactive values used inside effect in dependency array.
Return cleanup functions to clear timers and event subscriptions.

codeExamples.title: useEffect Subscription with Cleanup
codeExamples.description: Adding resize event listener and returning cleanup function.

mcqs.question: When does `useEffect` callback execute relative to component rendering?
options: After render commit phase is painted to screen asynchronously
mcqs.explanation: `useEffect` runs asynchronously after render paint commit completes, avoiding UI render blocking.

mcqs.question: When does `useEffect(fn, [])` with an empty dependency array run?
mcqs.explanation: Empty dependency array `[]` restricts effect execution to initial mount.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of returning a function from `useEffect`?
options: Registers a cleanup function to teardown listeners/timers on unmount or re-effect
mcqs.explanation: Returned cleanup function cleans up resources before re-effect execution or unmount.

mcqs.question: What happens if you update state `setCount(c => c + 1)` inside `useEffect(fn)` without a dependency array?
options: Infinite render loop crashing browser tab
mcqs.explanation: State update triggers re-render, which triggers effect, triggering state update in infinite loop.

mcqs.question: How should an AbortController be used inside `useEffect` for data fetching?
options: Instantiated before fetch, calling `controller.abort()` in returned cleanup function
mcqs.explanation: Calling `abort()` in effect cleanup cancels pending network requests if component unmounts mid-fetch.

title: useRef
summary: Mutable reference container, DOM node access, persisting values across renders without re-rendering.

explanation.overview: `useRef` returns a mutable ref object whose `.current` property persists across re-renders without triggering a component re-render when mutated.

sections.heading: Two Primary Use Cases of useRef
sections.content:
1. **DOM Node Access**: Attaching `ref={inputRef}` to JSX element to focus input, scroll, or measure layout.
2. **Instance Mutable Variable**: Storing timer IDs, previous state values, or flags without causing re-renders.
bulletPoints: DOM Access: `inputRef.current.focus()`.
Mutable State: Modifying `ref.current = newValue` does NOT trigger component re-render.
Persistence: Value survives component re-renders intact.

sections.heading: useRef vs useState
sections.content: Use `useState` when value changes should reflect visually in UI (triggers re-render). Use `useRef` for background tracking values not tied to rendering.
bulletPoints: useState: Mutation -> Re-render -> UI update.
useRef: Mutation -> Silent value update -> No re-render.

keyTakeaways: Mutating `ref.current` does NOT trigger component re-render.
Use `useRef` for direct DOM element access.
Use `useRef` to persist timer IDs or background mutable instance data.

codeExamples.title: DOM Access & Timer Ref
codeExamples.description: Focusing input element and storing timer ID with useRef.

mcqs.question: What happens when you mutate `ref.current = 10` returned by `useRef`?
options: Value updates silently without triggering component re-render
mcqs.explanation: Mutating `ref.current` updates referenced value without scheduling component re-renders.

mcqs.question: How do you attach a ref object `myRef` to a JSX `<input>` tag?
mcqs.explanation: React populates `myRef.current` with corresponding DOM node using `ref={myRef}` attribute.

mcqs.question: Which scenario is best suited for `useRef` instead of `useState`?
options: Storing setInterval timer ID for cleanup
mcqs.explanation: Timer IDs are background values not displayed in UI markup; `useRef` persists timer IDs without causing extra re-renders.

mcqs.question: What is initial `.current` value of `useRef(null)`?
mcqs.explanation: The argument passed to `useRef(initialValue)` initializes `ref.current` to that value (here `null`).

mcqs.question: Should you read or write `ref.current` during JSX render body execution?
options: No, avoid reading/writing `ref.current` during render phase because render body must remain pure
mcqs.explanation: Reading/writing refs during render phase violates component render purity; access refs in effects or event handlers.

title: useMemo
summary: Memoizing expensive calculations, referential equality optimization, dependency array cache invalidation.

explanation.overview: `useMemo` caches (memoizes) calculated result of an expensive function between component re-renders, recomputing only when dependencies change.

sections.heading: Caching Expensive Calculations
sections.content: Syntax: `const cachedValue = useMemo(() => computeExpensiveValue(a, b), [a, b])`. Skips recalculation on re-renders if `a` and `b` retain identical values.
bulletPoints: Performance: Avoids executing heavy loops/sorting algorithms on every render.
Dependency Array: Re-runs calculation function only when dependencies change.

sections.heading: Referential Equality Optimization
sections.content: Objects and arrays created during render get fresh reference pointers each render. `useMemo` preserves object reference stability to prevent unnecessary child re-renders.
bulletPoints: Reference Stability: Keeps object references stable for memoized child components (`React.memo`).
Premature Optimization Warning: Do not wrap simple inexpensive calculations in `useMemo` needlessly.

keyTakeaways: `useMemo` memoizes return value of a calculation.
Use for CPU-heavy data transformations or preserving object reference stability.
Avoid overusing `useMemo` for trivial calculations.

codeExamples.title: useMemo Expensive Filtering & Sorting
codeExamples.description: Memoizing filtered list sorting calculation.

mcqs.question: What is primary purpose of `useMemo` hook in React?
options: To cache result of expensive calculation between renders based on dependency array
mcqs.explanation: `useMemo` memoizes computed return values to prevent running expensive calculations on every render.

mcqs.question: When does `useMemo(() => fn(), [a, b])` re-execute the calculation function `fn`?
options: Only when value of dependency `a` or `b` changes
mcqs.explanation: React compares dependencies; `fn` executes only when one or more dependencies change.

mcqs.question: How can `useMemo` assist child component performance optimization using `React.memo`?
options: By preserving stable object/array reference pointers across parent re-renders
mcqs.explanation: Memoizing object props ensures child components receiving object props do not re-render due to new reference creation.

mcqs.question: Is `useMemo(() => a + b, [a, b])` recommended for simple 1+1 addition calculations?
options: No, overhead of hook memory allocation outweighs cost of simple addition
mcqs.explanation: Hook initialization and dependency comparison cost more than simple mathematical operations.

mcqs.question: What does `useMemo` return?
options: The memoized value returned by calculation function
mcqs.explanation: `useMemo` returns the evaluated result of its callback function.

title: useCallback
summary: Callback function memoization, referential equality for function props, pairing with React.memo.

explanation.overview: `useCallback` returns a memoized version of a callback function that only changes when its specified dependencies change.

sections.heading: Function Reference Equality Problem
sections.content: Functions declared inside component bodies are recreated on every render with new memory addresses. Passing inline functions to `React.memo` child components breaks memoization.
bulletPoints: Inline Functions: `const handleClick = () => {}` creates fresh function instance every render.
Solution: `useCallback(fn, deps)` returns identical function instance as long as `deps` match.

sections.heading: useCallback vs useMemo
sections.content: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is shorthand equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. `useCallback` caches function definition itself, while `useMemo` caches function return value.
bulletPoints: `useCallback`: Caches function reference.
`useMemo`: Caches calculated return value.

keyTakeaways: `useCallback` caches function definitions across renders.
Essential when passing callback functions as props to memoized (`React.memo`) children.
`useCallback(fn, deps)` is equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

codeExamples.title: useCallback with React.memo Child
codeExamples.description: Preventing unnecessary child component re-renders with useCallback.

mcqs.question: What does `useCallback` cache between renders?
mcqs.explanation: `useCallback` memoizes and returns identical function instance reference.

mcqs.question: What is main use case for wrapping a function prop in `useCallback`?
options: Prevent `React.memo` child components from re-rendering due to fresh function references
mcqs.explanation: Stable function references prevent memoized child components receiving function props from re-rendering.

mcqs.question: What is relationship between `useCallback(fn, deps)` and `useMemo`?
options: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`
mcqs.explanation: `useCallback` is shorthand for memoizing a function definition using `useMemo`.

mcqs.question: What happens if a state variable used inside `useCallback` function is omitted from dependency array?
options: Stale closure bug where function references outdated state value from initial render
mcqs.explanation: Omitting reactive values creates stale closure bugs where function reads old state.

mcqs.question: Does wrapping every function in component with `useCallback` automatically improve application performance?
options: No, adding `useCallback` blindly creates extra memory overhead and dependency array checks for no benefit without memoized child components
mcqs.explanation: `useCallback` has allocation cost; using it without memoized receiver components adds unnecessary overhead.

title: Context
summary: Solving prop drilling, createContext, Provider/Consumer, useContext hook, and context re-render performance.

explanation.overview: React Context enables sharing global data (theme, authentication, user settings) across component tree without explicit prop drilling.

sections.heading: createContext & useContext
sections.content: `const Context = createContext(defaultVal)` creates context object. `<Context.Provider value={data}>` supplies data to children, consumed via `useContext(Context)`.
bulletPoints: Provider: Wraps component subtree delivering shared state.
useContext: Consumes context value inside any nested child component.
Prop Drilling Solution: Bypasses intermediate component layers.

sections.heading: Context Re-render Performance Warning
sections.content: When Provider `value` changes, ALL components consuming that context re-render automatically, bypassing `React.memo`.
bulletPoints: Value Memoization: Wrap provider `value` in `useMemo` to prevent unnecessary object reference changes.
Context Splitting: Separate state context from dispatch/action context.

keyTakeaways: Context solves deep prop drilling for global data.
Consuming components re-render whenever provider value changes.
Memoize provider `value` object with `useMemo` to optimize render performance.

codeExamples.title: Theme Context Provider & Consumer
codeExamples.description: Creating theme context provider and consuming via useContext hook.

mcqs.question: What primary problem does React Context solve?
options: Prop drilling across deeply nested component trees
mcqs.explanation: Context provides shared data access directly without passing props through intermediate layers.

mcqs.question: Which hook consumes a React Context inside a functional component?
mcqs.explanation: `useContext(MyContext)` reads current context value from nearest matching Provider ancestor.

mcqs.question: What happens to consumer components when Context Provider `value` prop updates?
options: ALL components consuming that context re-render automatically
mcqs.explanation: When provider value updates, React re-renders every component consuming that context.

mcqs.question: Why should Context Provider `value={{ state, dispatch }}` object be wrapped in `useMemo`?
options: To keep value object reference stable across provider renders so consumers do not re-render unnecessarily
mcqs.explanation: Creating unmemoized inline objects inside provider value creates fresh references every render, forcing consumer re-renders.

mcqs.question: When is Context default argument `createContext(defaultValue)` used by a consumer?
options: Only when consumer component is rendered WITHOUT a matching Provider ancestor above it in DOM tree
mcqs.explanation: `defaultValue` is fallback used only if component consumes context outside matching Provider tree.

title: Custom hooks
summary: Extracting reusable stateful logic, `use` prefix naming rule, composability of standard built-in hooks.

explanation.overview: Custom Hooks are JavaScript functions whose names start with `use` that encapsulate reusable stateful logic composed of standard React built-in hooks.

sections.heading: Custom Hook Rules & Naming
sections.content: A custom hook must start with `use` prefix (`useFetch`, `useAuth`, `useLocalStorage`). Enforces React Linter Rules of Hooks.
bulletPoints: Encapsulation: Isolates stateful logic from UI rendering.
State Isolation: Calling a custom hook twice creates TWO completely independent state instances.
Rules of Hooks: Call hooks unconditionally at top level.

sections.heading: Extracting Logic Patterns
sections.content: Custom hooks extract data fetching, form handling, window event listeners, and media queries into clean reusable abstractions.
bulletPoints: Data Fetching: `useFetch(url)` returning `{ data, loading, error }`.
Form Handling: `useForm(initialValues)` returning `{ values, handleChange }`.

keyTakeaways: Custom hook names MUST start with `use`.
Custom hooks share stateful *logic*, NOT shared state instances.
Follow standard Rules of Hooks inside custom hooks.

codeExamples.title: useLocalStorage Custom Hook
codeExamples.description: Extracting persistent state synchronization with localStorage.

mcqs.question: What naming rule must custom React hooks strictly follow?
mcqs.explanation: React linter relies on `use` prefix to enforce Rules of Hooks inside custom hook functions.

mcqs.question: If Component A and Component B both invoke `const data = useFetch('/api')`, do they share state?
options: No, each hook invocation creates completely independent state variables
mcqs.explanation: Custom hooks reuse stateful *logic*; each component call gets isolated independent state.

mcqs.question: Can custom hooks invoke other built-in React hooks like `useState` and `useEffect`?
options: Yes, custom hooks compose built-in hooks and other custom hooks
mcqs.explanation: Custom hooks build higher-level abstractions by composing built-in React hooks.

mcqs.question: What should a custom hook return?
options: Any data structure (array tuple, object, primitive, function)
mcqs.explanation: Custom hooks can return arrays `[val, setVal]`, objects `{ data, loading }`, or any value.

mcqs.question: What is primary engineering advantage of custom hooks?
options: Separates complex stateful business logic from UI component rendering for clean testing and reuse
mcqs.explanation: Custom hooks decouple stateful business logic from UI view code.

title: Forms
summary: Form state handling, input event handlers, onSubmit validation, and form libraries.

explanation.overview: Form handling in React manages user input via component state, handling input `onChange` events and form `onSubmit` actions.

sections.heading: Handling Form Inputs in React
sections.content: Input fields bind their `value` to state and update state using `onChange` handlers. Multiple input fields can share a single state object using input `name` attributes.
bulletPoints: Controlled Binding: `<input value={state} onChange={e => setState(e.target.value)} />`.
Shared Handler: `const { name, value } = e.target; setForm(prev => ({ ...prev, [name]: value }))`.

sections.heading: Form Submission & Libraries
sections.content: Form submit events trigger default browser page reloads. Always invoke `e.preventDefault()` inside submit handlers.
bulletPoints: e.preventDefault(): Prevents browser full-page submission reload.
Form Libraries: React Hook Form / Formik simplify validation, error tracking, and touch state for complex forms.

keyTakeaways: Bind input values to React state for controlled inputs.
Call `e.preventDefault()` inside form submit handlers.
Use React Hook Form for large complex forms with schema validation.

codeExamples.title: Controlled Form with Shared Handler
codeExamples.description: Managing multiple input fields with single state object and preventDefault submit.

mcqs.question: Why is `e.preventDefault()` invoked inside form `onSubmit` handlers in React?
options: To prevent standard HTML browser submission which triggers full page reload
mcqs.explanation: `e.preventDefault()` stops default browser form navigation behavior, allowing JS submit handling.

mcqs.question: How do you access typed character string in an input `onChange` event `e`?
mcqs.explanation: `e.target` references target DOM input element; `.value` gets input string value.

mcqs.question: How can single state object `{ email: '', role: '' }` handle multiple inputs efficiently?
mcqs.explanation: Computed property name `[e.target.name]` dynamically updates state field matching input `name`.

mcqs.question: What is primary advantage of React Hook Form library over basic `useState` form state?
options: Uncontrolled performance architecture reducing unnecessary component re-renders on every keystroke
mcqs.explanation: React Hook Form uses uncontrolled refs to avoid re-rendering entire form on every character input.

mcqs.question: Which HTML input type requires checking `e.target.checked` instead of `e.target.value`?
mcqs.explanation: Checkbox input elements use boolean `e.target.checked` property.

title: Controlled/uncontrolled
summary: Controlled inputs (state driven) vs Uncontrolled inputs (DOM ref driven, defaultValue).

explanation.overview: Form elements can be Controlled (React state holds source of truth) or Uncontrolled (DOM retains internal input state accessed via ref).

sections.heading: Controlled Components
sections.content: Input `value` prop is bound to React state, and `onChange` updates state on every keystroke. React state acts as single source of truth.
bulletPoints: Single Source of Truth: React state controls displayed value.
Real-time Validation: Instant input sanitization, dynamic submit enabling.
Re-render: Component re-renders on every typed character.

sections.heading: Uncontrolled Components
sections.content: Input retains state inside browser DOM. Uses `defaultValue` for initial state and `useRef` to read value upon submit.
bulletPoints: DOM Source of Truth: Value read on demand via `ref.current.value`.
Performance: Zero component re-renders while user types.
Default Value: Uses `defaultValue` instead of `value` prop.

keyTakeaways: Controlled inputs use `value` + `onChange` (React state holds data).
Uncontrolled inputs use `defaultValue` + `useRef` (DOM holds data).
Controlled is standard; Uncontrolled offers performance optimization for large form fields.

codeExamples.title: Uncontrolled Component with useRef
codeExamples.description: Reading uncontrolled input value using useRef.

mcqs.question: What defines a Controlled input component in React?
options: Input `value` prop is bound to React state and updated via `onChange`
mcqs.explanation: In controlled components, React state is single source of truth for input `value`.

mcqs.question: How do you pass initial value to an Uncontrolled input without controlling its state?
mcqs.explanation: `defaultValue` initializes uncontrolled DOM inputs without locking `value` prop.

mcqs.question: What error occurs if an input transitions from uncontrolled (`value={undefined}`) to controlled (`value={state}`) after render?
options: React warning: A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled
mcqs.explanation: Switching from `undefined` value to defined state value triggers React uncontrolled-to-controlled warning.

mcqs.question: Which form element MUST always be an Uncontrolled component in HTML/React?
options: `<input type="file" />` (file input value is read-only in DOM security)
mcqs.explanation: File inputs are read-only due to browser security and must be accessed via refs as uncontrolled elements.

mcqs.question: What is performance advantage of Uncontrolled input components?
options: Component does not re-render on every user keystroke
mcqs.explanation: Uncontrolled inputs bypass React state update pipeline, avoiding component re-renders per keystroke.

title: Performance
summary: Profiling React apps, identifying waste renders, key prop rules, windowing/virtualization (react-window).

explanation.overview: React performance optimization eliminates wasteful component re-renders and reduces DOM element counts using profiling tools and list virtualization.

sections.heading: Identifying Waste Renders & React DevTools
sections.content: Waste renders occur when components execute render functions without producing visible DOM updates. Use React DevTools Profiler tab to record render timings and component re-render reasons.
bulletPoints: Profiler Tab: Visualizes flame graphs and commit render durations.
Highlight Updates: Highlights components on screen when re-rendering.
Common Causes: Unstable prop object references, parent re-renders.

sections.heading: List Virtualization (Windowing)
sections.content: Rendering thousands of DOM nodes causes severe UI lag. Virtualization libraries (`react-window`, `react-virtualized`) render ONLY DOM nodes visible inside current viewport window.
bulletPoints: Viewport Windowing: Render 20 items visible on screen out of 10,000 total dataset.
DOM Node Reduction: Keeps browser memory usage flat and scrolling smooth.

keyTakeaways: Use React DevTools Profiler to identify waste re-renders.
Use list virtualization (`react-window`) for long datasets.
Optimize state placement to prevent top-level tree re-renders.

codeExamples.title: List Virtualization Concept
codeExamples.description: Virtualizing large dataset rendering using react-window.

mcqs.question: What is a 'waste render' in React?
options: A component re-rendering when its rendered DOM output remains unchanged
mcqs.explanation: Waste render occurs when render phase calculates Virtual DOM that results in zero real DOM changes.

mcqs.question: What technique does 'List Virtualization' (Windowing) use to optimize rendering 50,000 items?
options: Renders ONLY items visible within current container viewport DOM window
mcqs.explanation: Virtualization renders only visible items in DOM, recycling container nodes as user scrolls.

mcqs.question: Which browser extension tool visualizes React component render durations and re-render triggers?
mcqs.explanation: React DevTools Profiler records flamegraphs of component render timing and state/prop update triggers.

mcqs.question: How does lifting state UP too high in component tree impact render performance?
options: Forces entire component subtree below state provider to re-render whenever state changes
mcqs.explanation: Lifting state high causes all descendant child components to re-render when state updates.

mcqs.question: What benefit does moving state DOWN to localized leaf components provide?
options: Isolates re-renders to only leaf components that require updated state
mcqs.explanation: Pushing state down prevents parent and sibling components from re-rendering on local state changes.

title: React.memo
summary: Higher-Order Component memoization, shallow prop comparison, custom areEqual comparator function.

explanation.overview: `React.memo` is a Higher-Order Component (HOC) that skips re-rendering a component if its props have not changed.

sections.heading: Shallow Prop Comparison
sections.content: `React.memo(Component)` performs shallow comparison (`Object.is`) of previous and current props. If props match, React reuses cached previous render output.
bulletPoints: Shallow Equal: Compares primitive prop values by value, objects/functions by reference pointer.
Optimization: Prevents child re-renders caused strictly by parent component updates.

sections.heading: Custom Comparator Function
sections.content: Pass second argument `areEqual(prevProps, nextProps)` to customize prop comparison logic.
bulletPoints: Syntax: `React.memo(Component, (prev, next) => boolean)`.
Return true: Props ARE equal -> SKIP render.
Return false: Props ARE NOT equal -> RE-RENDER component.

keyTakeaways: `React.memo` memoizes component render output based on prop comparison.
Performs shallow prop equality check by default.
Return `true` from custom `areEqual` comparator to SKIP re-render.

codeExamples.title: React.memo with Custom Comparator
codeExamples.description: Memoizing component with custom prop comparison function.

mcqs.question: What does `React.memo` do when wrapped around a component `const MemoComponent = React.memo(MyComponent)`?
options: Skips re-rendering component if props remain shallowly equal to previous render
mcqs.explanation: `React.memo` caches render output and skips re-rendering when props match.

mcqs.question: What comparison strategy does `React.memo` use by default for props?
options: Shallow equality check (`Object.is`) across prop keys
mcqs.explanation: `React.memo` performs shallow comparison on incoming prop object keys.

mcqs.question: Why does `<MemoChild onClick={() => {}} />` re-render every time parent re-renders despite `React.memo`?
options: Inline arrow function creates fresh function reference every render, failing shallow prop equality
mcqs.explanation: Inline functions create new object references every render, making shallow prop comparison return false.

mcqs.question: In `React.memo(Component, areEqual)`, what does returning `true` from `areEqual(prevProps, nextProps)` signify?
mcqs.explanation: Returning `true` tells React props are equal, skipping component re-render.

mcqs.question: Does `React.memo` prevent a component from re-rendering if its OWN internal `useState` state updates?
options: No, component STILL re-renders when its own internal state or context changes
mcqs.explanation: `React.memo` skips renders triggered by parent updates, but component still re-renders on its own state/context changes.

title: Lazy loading
summary: On-demand component dynamic imports, React.lazy, Suspense fallback boundaries.

explanation.overview: `React.lazy()` enables dynamic import of components on demand, deferring JavaScript bundle download until component is rendered.

sections.heading: React.lazy & Dynamic Import Syntax
sections.content: `const LazyComp = React.lazy(() => import('./LazyComp'))` dynamic import syntax loads bundle chunk lazily.
bulletPoints: Default Export Rule: Component targeted by `React.lazy` MUST be exported as `default`.
Code Splitting: Bundlers (Webpack, Vite) emit separate JS chunk file for lazy component.

sections.heading: Suspense Fallback Boundary
sections.content: Lazy components must be wrapped inside `<Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>`. Displays fallback UI while bundle JS downloads across network.
bulletPoints: Fallback UI: Displays spinner/skeleton placeholder while loading.
Boundary Placement: Place `<Suspense>` at route level or component level.

keyTakeaways: Use `React.lazy()` for on-demand component loading.
Target component MUST use default export (`export default`).
Always wrap lazy components inside `<Suspense fallback={...}>`.

codeExamples.title: React.lazy with Suspense Boundary
codeExamples.description: Lazy loading a heavy chart component with fallback spinner.

mcqs.question: What export format is required for components loaded via `React.lazy()`?
mcqs.explanation: `React.lazy` expects a promise resolving to a module with a `default` export.

mcqs.question: What component wrapper is REQUIRED around a `React.lazy` component to prevent crash while loading bundle?
mcqs.explanation: Lazy components require a `<Suspense>` parent boundary with a `fallback` UI prop.

mcqs.question: What does bundler (Vite/Webpack) generate when encountering `import('./MyComp')` in code?
options: Separate dynamic JavaScript chunk file loaded on demand
mcqs.explanation: Dynamic `import()` signals bundlers to split code into separate downloadable chunk files.

mcqs.question: What UI is rendered while dynamic bundle JS chunk is downloading over network?
options: The JSX element provided in `<Suspense fallback={...}>` prop
mcqs.explanation: Suspense renders its `fallback` prop content until dynamic import resolves.

mcqs.question: Where is lazy loading most commonly applied in single page applications?
options: At top-level application route boundaries (page routes)
mcqs.explanation: Route-level code splitting ensures users download code only for pages they actually visit.

title: Code splitting
summary: Reducing initial JavaScript bundle size, route-based splitting, dynamic import() statements.

explanation.overview: Code Splitting breaks massive single-file JavaScript bundles into smaller chunks loaded on demand, accelerating initial page load and Time to Interactive (TTI).

sections.heading: Initial Bundle Bloat Problem
sections.content: Single-page apps without code splitting force users to download entire application code upfront (admin dashboards, profile settings, editor modal scripts) before rendering initial homepage.
bulletPoints: Bundle Size Impact: High JS bundle size causes slow mobile load times.
Time to Interactive (TTI): Delay before page becomes responsive to user taps.

sections.heading: Route-Based & Feature-Based Splitting
sections.content: Split bundles at page routes or heavy feature modules (modal dialogs, rich text editors, PDF generators).
bulletPoints: Route-Based: Split `/dashboard`, `/settings`, `/admin` into isolated chunks.
Feature-Based: Dynamically import heavy libraries (e.g. `chart.js` or `pdfmake`) only when user clicks export.

keyTakeaways: Code splitting reduces initial JS bundle size.
Improves page load metrics (FCP, TTI).
Combine route-based code splitting with component feature splitting.

codeExamples.title: Feature-Based Dynamic Import
codeExamples.description: Dynamically importing heavy library only on button click.

mcqs.question: What primary performance metric does Code Splitting directly improve?
options: Initial page load time and Time to Interactive (TTI)
mcqs.explanation: Smaller initial JS bundles download and parse faster, improving initial page load time.

mcqs.question: Which JavaScript language feature enables code splitting at bundler level?
mcqs.explanation: Dynamic `import()` acts as code splitting entry point for bundlers.

mcqs.question: What is 'Route-Based Code Splitting'?
options: Creating separate JS bundle chunks corresponding to individual application page routes
mcqs.explanation: Route-based splitting loads JS bundle chunk for a specific route only when user navigates to it.

mcqs.question: When should heavy third-party libraries (e.g., chart or math rendering engines) be loaded?
options: Dynamically imported when user opens feature that requires library
mcqs.explanation: Dynamically importing heavy feature libraries keeps main bundle small.

mcqs.question: Which tool executes physical file chunk splitting during production builds?
mcqs.explanation: Module bundlers split JS code into distinct chunk files during build process.

title: Error boundaries
summary: Catching JavaScript errors in child tree, componentDidCatch, getDerivedStateFromError, fallback UI.

explanation.overview: Error Boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in child component tree, log errors, and display fallback UI instead of crashing whole application screen.

sections.heading: Class Component Requirement & Lifecycle Methods
sections.content: Error Boundaries MUST be Class components because React currently lacks a functional hook equivalent for error boundary lifecycles.
bulletPoints: `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)`: Renders fallback UI state.
`componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo)`: Logs error details to reporting services (Sentry, LogRocket).
Scope: Catches errors during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors of child components.

sections.heading: What Error Boundaries Do NOT Catch
sections.content:
Error Boundaries do NOT catch errors inside:
1. Asynchronous code (`setTimeout`, promise callbacks).
2. Event handlers (`onClick` - use standard `try/catch`).
3. Server-side rendering (SSR).
4. Errors thrown inside error boundary component itself.
bulletPoints: Event Handlers: Use `try...catch` inside button click handlers.
Async Callbacks: Handle promise rejections explicitly.

keyTakeaways: Error Boundaries catch render errors in child component subtrees.
MUST be Class components implementing `getDerivedStateFromError` or `componentDidCatch`.
Do NOT catch errors inside event handlers or async callbacks.

codeExamples.title: Error Boundary Class Component
codeExamples.description: Implementing Error Boundary fallback UI and Sentry error logging.

mcqs.question: Why must Error Boundaries be implemented as Class components in React currently?
options: React lacks functional hook equivalents for `componentDidCatch` or `getDerivedStateFromError`
mcqs.explanation: Error boundary lifecycle methods (`componentDidCatch`, `getDerivedStateFromError`) exist only in class components.

mcqs.question: Which static lifecycle method updates state to render fallback UI after error occurs in child component?
mcqs.explanation: `getDerivedStateFromError` returns state object updating component to display fallback UI.

mcqs.question: Does an Error Boundary catch uncaught exceptions thrown inside a button `onClick` event handler?
options: No, Error Boundaries do NOT catch errors inside event handlers (use try/catch)
mcqs.explanation: Event handler errors do not occur during render phase; use standard `try/catch` inside event handlers.

mcqs.question: What happens to React UI tree if an uncaught render error occurs WITHOUT an Error Boundary?
options: Entire React application unmounts, presenting a blank white screen
mcqs.explanation: Uncaught render errors unmount the entire component tree, causing blank screens.

mcqs.question: Which lifecycle method is used inside Error Boundary to log error stacktraces to external logging services?
mcqs.explanation: `componentDidCatch` receives error details and component stack trace for logging to telemetry services.

title: SSR/CSR basics
summary: Client-Side Rendering vs Server-Side Rendering, hydration, SEO implications, and Next.js basics.

explanation.overview: Single-Page Applications use Client-Side Rendering (CSR) or Server-Side Rendering (SSR) to render UI markup and manage user interactivity.

sections.heading: Client-Side Rendering (CSR)
sections.content:
Browser downloads empty HTML shell `
` and large JS bundle. Browser JS executes, fetches data, and constructs DOM client-side.
bulletPoints: Initial HTML: Empty shell div container.
Pros: Smooth client page transitions, lower server CPU load.
Cons: Slow initial paint (FCP), poor SEO without client JS execution.

sections.heading: Server-Side Rendering (SSR) & Hydration
sections.content: Server generates fully populated HTML string per request. Browser displays HTML immediately, followed by React **Hydration** attaching event listeners to static markup.
bulletPoints: Initial HTML: Fully populated content markup.
Hydration: React attaches event listeners to pre-rendered HTML DOM.
SEO: Web crawlers read fully populated HTML content instantly.

keyTakeaways: CSR renders DOM in browser via JS; SSR pre-renders HTML on server per request.
SSR provides immediate FCP and superior SEO crawler indexability.
Hydration connects JS event listeners to server-rendered HTML DOM.

codeExamples.title: Hydration Concept
codeExamples.description: Hydrating server-rendered HTML using ReactDOM.hydrateRoot.

mcqs.question: What does browser initial HTML response contain in pure Client-Side Rendering (CSR)?
options:
Empty container shell `
` and script bundle tag
mcqs.explanation: CSR sends minimal HTML shell; JavaScript builds entire UI client-side.

mcqs.question: What is 'Hydration' in React SSR?
options: Process where client React attaches event listeners and state to server-rendered static HTML DOM
mcqs.explanation: Hydration preserves server-rendered HTML markup while attaching interactive JS event handlers.

mcqs.question: Why does Server-Side Rendering (SSR) offer better Search Engine Optimization (SEO)?
options: Search engine web crawlers receive fully populated HTML content immediately without requiring JS execution
mcqs.explanation: Search engine crawlers read pre-rendered HTML content directly without running client JS.

mcqs.question: What causes a 'Hydration Mismatch Error' in SSR applications?
options: Server-rendered HTML output differs from initial client render output (e.g. using window.innerWidth or new Date() on render)
mcqs.explanation: Hydration errors occur when client initial render tree does not match server pre-rendered HTML tree.

mcqs.question: Which modern React framework simplifies SSR, SSG, and Server Components?
mcqs.explanation: Next.js is the leading React framework for Server-Side Rendering and static site generation.
